title: How do you validate that UI-displayed data matches the database (extract UI data → run the source-of-truth DB query → compare → report mismatches), and what pitfalls must you handle (data/date/currency formatting, nulls, case sensitivity, pagination, and large datasets)?
shortTitle: Validating that UI-displayed data matches the database

s1_definition.profdef: UI-to-database validation confirms that what the application shows a user matches the authoritative data in the database. The approach is to extract the values displayed in the UI, run the source-of-truth query against the database, normalize both sides to a comparable form, compare them, and report any mismatches. The important pitfalls are formatting differences in dates, numbers, and currency, null handling, case sensitivity, pagination so you compare complete sets, and large datasets where you must sample, paginate, or compare in bulk rather than row by row.
s1_definition.analogy: When Rajesh opens his statement on the National Bank of India app and sees a balance of nine hundred fifty thousand rupees and a list of transactions, a tester must be sure the screen is telling the truth, that it exactly matches what the bank's ledger database actually holds. So the tester reads the numbers off the screen, asks the database directly for the same account, and compares. The trap is that the screen might show the rupees as "9,50,000.00" while the database stores a plain number 950000.00, or the date as "30 Oct 2026" while the database stores a timestamp, so the tester must line them up fairly before comparing, and must be careful with empty values, capitalization, and the fact that the screen shows only one page of a long transaction list.
s1_definition.oneliner: Extract the UI values, query the database as the source of truth, normalize both sides for formatting, nulls, and case, then compare and report mismatches, while handling pagination and large datasets so you compare complete, fairly formatted data.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** UI-to-database validation confirms that what the application shows a user matches the authoritative data in the database. The approach is to extract the values displayed in the UI, run the source-of-truth query against the database, normalize both sides to a comparable form, compare them, and report any mismatches. The important pitfalls are formatting differences in dates, numbers, and currency, null handling, case sensitivity, pagination so you compare complete sets, and large datasets where you must sample, paginate, or compare in bulk rather than row by row.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** When Rajesh opens his statement on the National Bank of India app and sees a balance of nine hundred fifty thousand rupees and a list of transactions, a tester must be sure the screen is telling the truth, that it exactly matches what the bank's ledger database actually holds. So the tester reads the numbers off the screen, asks the database directly for the same account, and compares. The trap is that the screen might show the rupees as "9,50,000.00" while the database stores a plain number 950000.00, or the date as "30 Oct 2026" while the database stores a timestamp, so the tester must line them up fairly before comparing, and must be careful with empty values, capitalization, and the fact that the screen shows only one page of a long transaction list.

**One line to remember:** Extract the UI values, query the database as the source of truth, normalize both sides for formatting, nulls, and case, then compare and report mismatches, while handling pagination and large datasets so you compare complete, fairly formatted data.

sections.s2_technical:
The core workflow is extract, query, normalize, compare, report. First you extract the displayed values from the UI using stable locators, reading text such as the balance, the account holder name, and each transaction row. Second you run the source-of-truth query directly against the database for the same entity, for example selecting the balance and transactions for that account, treating the database as the authority because the UI is a view over it. Third, and most important, you normalize both sides into a canonical comparable form before comparing, because the UI almost always formats data for humans while the database stores raw values. Fourth you compare the normalized values, and fifth you report precise mismatches showing the field, the UI value, and the database value so a developer can act.

The pitfalls are where most naive comparisons fail. Formatting of numbers and currency is the biggest: the UI may show grouping separators, a currency symbol, and a fixed number of decimals, while the database stores a plain decimal, so you must strip symbols and separators and compare numeric values with the correct scale, and crucially compare money as BigDecimal with a defined scale rather than as strings or floating-point, so that 950000 and 950000.00 compare equal and no rounding error creeps in. Date and time formatting is similar: the UI shows a localized, human-readable date while the database stores a timestamp possibly in a different time zone, so you parse both to a canonical instant or date and account for time zone before comparing. Null handling matters because the UI may render a null as an empty string, a dash, or the literal text "null", while the database returns an actual null, so you define a single rule for what null maps to on each side. Case sensitivity bites on text comparisons, because the UI may title-case a name the database stores in upper case, so you decide whether the comparison is case-sensitive and normalize accordingly, being careful not to hide a real casing bug.

Pagination and large datasets are the structural pitfalls. The UI typically shows one page of a long list, so comparing the visible page against the full database result will report false mismatches; you either paginate through the UI to assemble the complete set, or constrain the database query to the same page and ordering, and you must match the sort order exactly because two correct sets in different orders will appear different. For large datasets, row-by-row comparison through the UI is too slow and brittle, so you compare in bulk: extract the UI data into a structured collection, pull the database result into the same structure, and compare as sets or maps keyed by a stable identifier, or compare an aggregate such as a count and a checksum first and only drill into rows on mismatch. The senior nuances are to always treat the database as the source of truth, to normalize before comparing rather than comparing raw strings, to key comparisons on a stable identifier so order and pagination do not create noise, to compare money and dates in their proper types, and to report mismatches with enough detail, field, UI value, database value, and key, that the result is actionable. Done well, this catches a whole class of defects where the UI silently shows stale, mis-formatted, or wrong data even though the underlying system is correct, which in a bank directly affects customer trust.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — Rajesh's statement screen shows a balance formatted as a grouped currency string, while the ledger stores a plain decimal. A naive string comparison would wrongly flag a mismatch, so the tester must normalize both to BigDecimal. This is exactly the currency-formatting pitfall.

Problem 2 — The transaction dates appear as human-readable strings on screen but as timestamps in the database, and the name is title-cased on screen but upper-cased in storage. The tester must normalize dates to a canonical form and handle case. These are the date and case pitfalls.

Problem 3 — The screen shows only the first page of transactions, so the comparison must align pagination and ordering or compare keyed sets, not the visible page against the whole table. This is exactly the pagination pitfall.

In the mini-project we model a UI reader and a database source, a normalizer that canonicalizes money, dates, nulls, and case, and a comparator that reports keyed mismatches. We define a `Row` of displayed data, a `UiData` and `DbData` source, a `DataNormalizer`, and a `UiDbComparator`.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: two transactions shown in the UI with grouped currency, human-readable dates, and title-cased names, and the same two in the database with plain decimals, ISO dates, and upper-case names.

Step 1: The normalizer converts each UI money string, stripping the symbol and separators, into a BigDecimal with scale two, so "9,50,000.00" becomes 950000.00.

Step 2: The normalizer parses each date, the UI "30 Oct 2026" and the database "2026-10-30", into the same LocalDate, removing the formatting difference.

Step 3: The normalizer upper-cases both the UI and database names so the case difference does not cause a false mismatch.

Step 4: The comparator indexes both sides by transaction id and compares keyed records, which avoids false mismatches from pagination or ordering. Both rows match, so it reports all match.

Step 5: The negative run changes the UI amount for the second transaction to fifty-five thousand while the database holds fifty thousand, and the comparator reports a precise mismatch showing the id, the UI value, and the database value, demonstrating that real discrepancies are caught.

Final output:

```
2026-10-30 09:28:30 [INFO] === UI vs DB comparison (normalized) ===
2026-10-30 09:28:30 [INFO] MATCH id=TXN-1
2026-10-30 09:28:30 [INFO] MATCH id=TXN-2
2026-10-30 09:28:30 [INFO] Overall: ALL MATCH (UI reflects source of truth)
2026-10-30 09:28:30 [INFO] === Negative: UI shows wrong amount ===
2026-10-30 09:28:30 [INFO] MATCH id=TXN-1
2026-10-30 09:28:30 [SEVERE] MISMATCH id=TXN-2 ui={TXN-2, PRIYA SHARMA, 55000.00, 2026-10-29} db={TXN-2, PRIYA SHARMA, 50000.00, 2026-10-29}
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  UI screen (formatted for humans)
    │ extract via stable locators
    ▼
  Raw UI values: "9,50,000.00", "30 Oct 2026", "Rajesh Kumar"
    │                                   ▲
    │ normalize                         │ query source of truth
    ▼                                   │
  Canonical Row {amount:BigDecimal, date:LocalDate, name:UPPER}
    │                                   │
    │          DB: 950000, 2026-10-30, "RAJESH KUMAR"
    │                 │ normalize
    ▼                 ▼
  Keyed compare (by id) → MATCH / MISMATCH / MISSING / EXTRA
    │
    ▼
  Report: field, UI value, DB value, key
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Validating that UI data matches the database is a reconciliation task, and I follow a fixed workflow: extract the values displayed in the UI, run the source-of-truth query against the database, normalize both sides into a comparable canonical form, compare, and report precise mismatches. The database is always the authority because the UI is just a view over it. The step that separates a reliable check from a noisy one is normalization, because the UI almost always formats data for humans while the database stores raw values.

The pitfalls are exactly where naive comparisons fail. Currency and number formatting is the biggest, so I strip grouping separators and currency symbols and compare money as BigDecimal with a defined scale, which makes nine hundred fifty thousand and 950000.00 compare equal and avoids floating-point rounding. Dates differ because the UI shows a localized human-readable date while the database stores a timestamp, possibly in a different time zone, so I parse both to a canonical date or instant and account for the zone. Nulls differ because the UI may show an empty string, a dash, or the word null while the database returns an actual null, so I define one mapping rule per side. Case sensitivity bites on text like names, so I decide whether the comparison is case-sensitive and normalize, being careful not to mask a genuine casing bug. And the structural pitfalls are pagination and large datasets: the UI shows one page of a long list, so I either paginate the UI to assemble the full set or constrain the database query to the same page and exact sort order, and for large data I compare keyed sets or maps by a stable identifier, or compare counts and checksums first and drill into rows only on mismatch.

At the National Bank of India I built a Playwright plus JDBC reconciliation test for the statement screen that normalized money, dates, and names and compared transactions keyed by transaction identifier. It caught a real defect where the UI showed a stale cached balance that did not match the ledger after a late-settling transaction, something a human glancing at the screen would never have noticed. Being able to describe the extract-query-normalize-compare-report flow and to name each formatting, null, case, and pagination pitfall and how I handle it is what shows an interviewer I can prove the screen tells the truth, which in a bank is a matter of customer trust.
